raw_text:
Ronald Cotton — eyewitness misidentification and DNA exoneration (Burlington, North Carolina)

On July 29, 1984, at around three in the morning, a man broke into the apartment of Jennifer Thompson, a twenty-two-year-old college student in Burlington, North Carolina, and sexually assaulted her. She escaped through the back door. Later that same night, a second woman was sexually assaulted nearby.

Investigators recovered foam rubber at Thompson's apartment and a drop of blood at the second crime scene. Thompson described her attacker to police as "a tall, light-skinned Black man" and worked with them to build a composite sketch. She was shown a set of mugshots that included Ronald Cotton, a twenty-two-year-old local man with prior arrests for breaking and entering and attempted assault. She identified him from the photographic array. Cotton was arrested on July 31, 1984, and police found tennis shoes with foam insoles at his home. Shown a live lineup afterward, Thompson picked Cotton again, and her confidence in the identification grew with each procedure that confirmed the one before it.

At trial in January 1985, Cotton was convicted of first-degree rape, first-degree burglary, and first-degree sexual offense, and sentenced to life plus fifty years. The second victim had identified a different suspect, and evidence of that identification was kept from the jury.

In 1987 the North Carolina Supreme Court reversed the conviction, holding that evidence of the second victim identifying a different man should have been admitted. Cotton was retried in November 1987. By then both women identified him as their attacker. The defense sought to present Bobby Poole as an alternate suspect: Poole's blood type matched evidence recovered from the second assault, and while imprisoned he had confessed to both crimes. The court refused to allow the jury to hear it. Cotton was convicted again, this time of both assaults, and sentenced to life plus fifty-four years.

In the spring of 1995, at the request of the defense, the Burlington Police Department turned over all of the physical evidence in the case, including the rape kits from both victims, for DNA testing. The testing excluded Ronald Cotton and matched Bobby Poole, who was by then already serving a life sentence for other sexual assaults. The charges against Cotton were dismissed on June 30, 1995, after he had served ten and a half years. On July 11, 1995, Poole pleaded guilty to both rapes and received seventy years on top of the sentence he was already serving.

Nothing in the case turned on a fabricated document, a coerced statement, or a manufactured laboratory result. The identification procedures were conducted in the ordinary way and the two women who identified Ronald Cotton believed what they said. The certainty they carried into the courtroom was real. It was also wrong. The composite sketch, the photographic array, the live lineup, and eleven years of retelling each reinforced a memory that had fixed on the wrong man early and hardened around him. What the trials recorded as two independent eyewitnesses converging on one suspect was one mistaken recognition, confirmed and amplified by the procedures meant to test it.

Cotton received $110,000 in compensation from the state. He went to work at a laboratory company, married, and had a child. He and Jennifer Thompson-Cannino met for the first time after his exoneration, became friends, and began traveling together to speak about wrongful conviction and the reform of eyewitness identification procedures. They published a joint account of the case, Picking Cotton: Our Memoir of Injustice and Redemption, in 2009.

act_type.rationale: A third-person factual recounting of the Cotton case — dates, procedures, rulings, DNA results — asserting what happened as true. No performative act changes reality by being uttered; it reports and characterizes.

cooperative.implicature: The procedures that felt like corroboration were actually one error compounding itself; sincerity is not accuracy.

transmission.rationale: A preserved, structured account moving a documented case from past to future — culminating in a published memoir and reform advocacy. Its function is durable record-keeping, not restricted disclosure or momentary broadcast.

resonance.surface: Two independent eyewitnesses converging on one guilty man, carrying real, hard-won certainty into court — apparent alignment of victim, memory, and verdict.
resonance.underlying: A single mistaken recognition, fixed early and hardened by each confirming procedure, sending an innocent man to prison for over a decade.

authority.source: Courts, police departments, state compensation, DNA labs — the formal legal-institutional record.
authority.rationale: The act is grounded entirely in institutional, legal, and forensic authority: convictions, appellate reversals, evidentiary rulings, and official exoneration.

utility.rationale: Primarily meaning-making — it turns a case into a lesson about how sincere memory fails. Secondarily instructional, aimed at reforming eyewitness identification procedures.

social_field.rationale: Public-facing educational narrative in open discourse: low binding by shared roles, weak membership identity. It addresses a general audience rather than an in-group under strict rules.

act_position.rationale: The text is a retrospective third-party summary that narrates and analyzes the Cotton case from outside it, leaving the events unchanged.

conflict.rationale: A sovereign legal apparatus, acting in good faith through ordinary procedures, produced a self-reinforcing false certainty in which each confirming step hardened a single mistaken recognition, so structural harm occurred and was recorded as legitimate convergence rather than error.
